question: Infrasound is sound with a frequency below the lower limit of human hearing. Widely occurring in nature (for example, in earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, etc.), it is also artificially generated by wind turbines. Since infrasound propagates over vast distances with virtually no losses, it can affect the whole body, disrupting cellular processes in humans and animals. As a result, it can also be used as a weapon.

1 A recent study from the infrasound working group at the Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz found that areas where wind energy has expanded massively are experiencing a markedly higher rate of newly diagnosed cardiovascular disease (heart arrhythmias, cardiac insufficiency).

2Infrasound can cause balance disturbances, dizziness, nausea, sleep disorders, changes to blood flow, an increase in blood pressure, and damage to lungs and internal organs. There can also be adverse psychological effects, particularly reduced concentration.
3 In the meantime, three judgments have been handed down by courts in Belgium and France4, awarding local residents compensation for wind-turbine-induced health problems.5 1.
Why has it trivialised the dangers associated with wind turbines up to now, and how will it make people aware of these dangers in future?
What is its view of the court judgments from Belgium and France acknowledging health problems caused by wind turbines?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.10.2026) 1. The Commission takes potential health effects of wind turbines seriously, including in relation to infrasound, which also comes from many natural and other human-made sources. In 2018, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued the Environmental Noise Guidelines for the European Region1, which include recommendations on wind turbine noise.

It was acknowledged that wind turbines can generate infrasound or lower frequencies of sound than traffic sources. While the WHO recommended2 keeping audible wind turbine noise below 45 decibel level to prevent annoyance and sleep disturbance, there were no specific limits or guidelines provided regarding the issue of infrasound due to the lack of sufficient scientific evidence.

While more recent studies enhance understanding of the acoustic characteristics of wind turbines, including low-frequency sound and infrasound, additional research would be needed to better define potential health risks. 2.

In line with the precautionary principle set out in the Treaty of the Functioning of the EU and applicable Union legislation3, certain projects, including wind farms, shall be subject to relevant assessments before an authorisation or permit is granted so that any likely significant impacts on various environmental factors, including population and human health and biodiversity are avoided, prevented or reduced.
Authorisation of such projects is the responsibility of Member States which must ensure compliance with relevant Union and national legislation for their construction and operation.
